stimulus.title: A weather station that samples every 16 milliseconds
stimulus.body:
A weather station records a temperature every 16 ms. Each reading is stamped with the elapsed time in milliseconds since the shift began, so during the first 128 ms the eight keys that are stored are 16, 32, 48, 64, 80, 96, 112 and 128.

The readings are held in a hash table of m buckets. The hash function is h(k) = k mod m, and collisions are resolved by linear probing: a key whose bucket is already occupied is placed in the next bucket that is free, wrapping around to bucket 0 if the end of the table is reached. A lookup follows the same sequence and stops when it finds the key or reaches an empty bucket.

Two table sizes are under consideration, m = 16 and m = 17. A colleague has also suggested doubling the table to m = 32, on the grounds that a larger table must be faster.

provenance.inspired_by: UK A-Level Computer Science — hash tables and collision resolution (linear probing)
provenance.adaptation: The source archetype is the A-Level theory question that asks a candidate to compute a load factor and describe linear probing. Three of the four permitted changes were made. The structure was changed from a single table to a comparison between two table sizes, so the answer is a relation between two results rather than one result. The given-versus-asked was inverted: the source supplies a key set that spreads and asks for the load factor, while this item supplies a key set that does not spread and asks the candidate to discover that the load factor is the wrong instrument. The reasoning chain was extended from "apply the formula" to "test the formula's predictive power, then test a repair". The context, the sampling-interval framing, all the numbers, the figure and the part decomposition are new, and no wording is reproduced from any specification or textbook.

figure.caption: The same eight keys in a table of 16 buckets and a table of 17 buckets. The vertical axis is the number of keys stored in each bucket.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The load factor is the first quantity a candidate reaches for, and it is nearly identical in two tables whose lookup costs differ by a factor of eight, so a correct calculation of the wrong quantity yields a confident and wrong conclusion.
questions.question: Evaluate whether the load factor is a reliable predictor of the cost of a lookup in this table. Work in probes, where one probe examines one bucket. Assume the eight keys are inserted in increasing order, that no key is ever deleted, and that the table is empty before the first insert.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the bucket index that each of the eight keys hashes to when m = 16, and state the number of probes needed to insert each of those keys.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the load factor of the table at m = 16 and at m = 17, and determine how many of the m buckets each table can ever reach with these eight keys. Give both reachable shares as percentages to two decimal places.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine the number of probes needed to look up the key 128, and the number needed to establish that the key 144 is absent, in each of the m = 16 and m = 17 tables. Explain why the two load factors do not predict the difference you find.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Your colleague proposes doubling the table from m = 16 to m = 32. Determine the load factor and the reachable-bucket share at m = 32, and justify whether the proposal addresses the problem you identified in part (c).

questions.answer:
**Part (a).** Every key is a multiple of 16, because 16 = 16 x 1, 32 = 16 x 2 and so on up to 128 = 16 x 8. So for every one of the eight keys k mod 16 = 0. **(M1)** All eight keys hash to bucket 0. **(A1)**

Linear probing then places them in consecutive buckets starting at 0: the first key finds bucket 0 free and takes it, the second finds it occupied and takes bucket 1, and so on. The probes needed are therefore 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 and 8, and the total for the eight inserts is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 = 36. **(A1)**

The finished table holds 16 in bucket 0, 32 in bucket 1, 48 in bucket 2, and so on up to 128 in bucket 7. Buckets 8 to 15 are empty.

**Part (b).** At m = 16 the table holds 8 keys in 16 buckets, so the load factor is 8 / 16 = 0.50. **(M1)(A1)** At m = 17 it is 8 / 17 = 0.470588..., which is 0.47 to two decimal places. **(A1)**

The reachable share is a different quantity. At m = 16 only bucket 0 is ever reached, so 1 of the 16 buckets is in play: 1 / 16 = 6.25%. **(M1)(A1)**

At m = 17 the keys hash to 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11, 10 and 9 — eight distinct buckets, because 17 shares no factor with the key step of 16, so each successive key lands in the bucket before the previous one. So 8 of the 17 buckets are reachable: 8 / 17 = 47.06%. **(A1)**

It is worth noticing that at m = 17 the reachable share and the load factor are the same number, 47.06%, because every key occupies a bucket of its own. That coincidence does not hold at m = 16, where the two quantities are 0.50 and 0.0625 — a factor of eight apart. The two quantities are equal only when no two keys collide, which is exactly the case in which there is nothing to predict.

**Part (c).** At m = 16 the key 128 was the eighth key inserted, so it sits at the end of a run of eight occupied buckets that begins at bucket 0. A successful search for 128 examines buckets 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7: eight probes. **(M1)(A1)**

The key 144 is also 0 mod 16, so it too begins at bucket 0. It must examine all eight occupied buckets and then bucket 8, which is empty, before it can conclude that the key is absent: nine probes. **(A1)**

At m = 17, 128 mod 17 = 9 and bucket 9 holds 128 alone, so the successful search costs one probe. And 144 mod 17 = 8, and bucket 8 is empty, so the unsuccessful search also costs one probe. **(M1)(A1)**

The two load factors are 0.50 and 0.47, differing by 0.03, or about 6% of either value. Yet the successful search costs eight times as much in one table as in the other, and the unsuccessful search nine times as much. A quantity that differs by 6% cannot account for a cost that differs by 700%. The load factor describes how full the table is; what governs the cost here is how the keys *distribute*, and with a key step of 16 and a table size of 16 the distribution is degenerate — every key competes for one bucket. The load factor is a correct measure of a real property that happens not to be the property that decides this question.

**Part (d).** At m = 32 the keys 32, 64, 96 and 128 are all 0 mod 32, and 16, 48, 80 and 112 are all 16 mod 32. So the keys occupy exactly two buckets, 0 and 16, each holding four keys. **(M1)(A1)**

The load factor is 8 / 32 = 0.25, exactly half of 0.50. **(A1)** The reachable share is 2 / 32 = 1 / 16 = 6.25%, which is unchanged from m = 16. **(A1)**

So the proposal does reduce the worst-case successful search from eight probes to four, and the unsuccessful search from nine to five, because each run of colliding keys is now half as long. But it does not address the defect found in part (c). The table can still reach only one sixteenth of its buckets, and it has paid for that with twice as much memory. Doubling the table halves the *consequence* of the clustering while leaving its *cause* untouched, and the cause is that the table size shares a factor with the key step. Changing the size to 17 removes that shared factor; doubling it to 32 does not, and doubling it again to 64 would not either. The general rule is that the number of buckets a key set can reach is m divided by the greatest common divisor of m and the key step, capped by the number of keys — 1 at m = 16, 2 at m = 32, 8 at m = 17.
questions.markscheme_notes:
**(a)** M1 for recognising that every key is a multiple of 16 and therefore 0 mod 16. A1 for all eight keys in bucket 0. A1 for the probe counts 1 to 8, or for the total of 36, or for the finished table. A candidate who writes "k mod 16 = k" has not seen the divisibility and scores nothing in this part.

**(b)** M1 for the load factor definition, A1 for 0.50. A1 for 0.47 (accept 0.4706, accept 8/17). M1 for the idea that the reachable share is counted in buckets rather than keys. A1 for 6.25% at m = 16. A1 for 47.06% at m = 17. Do not award the last A1 for an answer that reports 100% or 8/8: the denominator is the number of buckets, not the number of keys.

**(c)** M1 for the correct probe count on one of the two tables, A1 for eight probes to find 128 at m = 16. A1 for nine probes to establish that 144 is absent. M1 for the corresponding m = 17 figures, A1 for both being one probe. The explanation must connect the near-equal load factors to the very different costs; a candidate who reports the numbers but says only that the tables are "different" has not answered the question and should lose the final A1.

**(d)** M1 for the two occupied buckets, A1 for identifying buckets 0 and 16 with four keys each. A1 for 0.25. A1 for the reachable share staying at 6.25%. The justification must separate the halved worst case from the unchanged reachable share. Accept a conclusion either way provided the two quantities are distinguished; a candidate who claims the reachable share improves has not done part (b) correctly.
questions.explanation:
This item is built on a quantity that is correct, standard and useless for the question asked. The load factor is the first thing a prepared candidate computes when a hash table is described, and here it is genuinely informative about one thing — how full the table is — while being almost silent about the thing that matters, which is how long a lookup takes.

The trap is laid by making the two load factors nearly equal in the two tables whose costs are furthest apart. At m = 16 and m = 17 the load factors are 0.50 and 0.47, a difference of 0.03. A candidate who reasons "the load factors are almost the same, so the tables perform almost the same" has done the arithmetic correctly and drawn the wrong conclusion, and nothing in the arithmetic will warn them. The correct answer needs a second quantity — how many buckets the key set can reach — that is not in the standard vocabulary of load factor and probe length.

The reason the two diverge is structural. The keys are 16, 32, ..., 128, so every key is a multiple of 16, and the number of buckets a key set can reach is m divided by the greatest common divisor of m and the key step. At m = 16 that divisor is 16 and the table has one usable bucket; at m = 17 it is 1 and the table has eight, one per key. The load factor cannot see this because it counts keys and buckets, not residues.

Part (d) is where the item earns its label rather than merely stating it. Doubling the table halves the load factor and halves the worst-case probe count, so a candidate who trusted the load factor will find that it *worked* — and will conclude that the proposal is sound. It is not, because the reachable share does not move at all: 2 of 32 buckets is 6.25%, exactly what 1 of 16 was. The load factor improved, the probe length improved, and the underlying defect is untouched. A single measurement that moves in the right direction is not evidence that the cause has been addressed, and the second measurement — the one nobody thinks to take — is what shows it.

verification.method: Both tables were simulated in Python: the eight keys were inserted into an array of m buckets using k mod m with linear probing, and the probe count for each insert, each successful lookup and each unsuccessful lookup was recorded rather than assumed. At m = 16 every key lands in bucket 0 and the probe counts are 1 to 8; at m = 17 the keys land in buckets 16 down to 9 and every lookup costs one probe; at m = 32 the keys occupy buckets 0 and 16 only. The reachable-bucket counts were computed by enumeration of the residues, not by inspection.
solution_skeleton: note that every key is a multiple of 16 and therefore hashes to bucket 0
place the eight keys in consecutive buckets by linear probing and count the probes
compute the load factor for each table size
count how many distinct buckets the key set can reach, not how many keys it holds
compare the lookup costs at the two sizes and find they differ by a factor of eight
halve the table, observe that the reachable share does not move, and name the governing quantity as m divided by its greatest common divisor with the key step

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compute the load factor for both tables, find 0.50 against 0.47, and conclude that the two tables perform almost identically so neither size needs changing.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The two load factors differ by 0.03 while the successful-search costs differ by a factor of eight, because what governs the cost is how many buckets the key set can reach, and at m = 16 that number is one.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Reporting that m = 17 offers no real improvement over m = 16, and that doubling the table to m = 32 is a sound repair because it halves the load factor.

stimulus.title: A logger that keeps its readings in a singly linked list
stimulus.body:
A data logger keeps its most recent readings in a singly linked list. Each node holds one reading in a field called data and one pointer in a field called next that points at the following node. The last node's next pointer is None, and the whole list is reached through a single variable head that points at the first node. No node holds a pointer to the node before it.

After four readings have been logged the list is A -> B -> C -> D, where A is the node that head points at and D is the last node.

A method remove(node) is added to the class. It is called with a reference to the node that should be deleted and with nothing else: it is not given head, and it is not told where the node sits in the list.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The method is handed the object that must disappear but the only pointer that has to change belongs to a different object that the method cannot reach, so the obvious implementation is impossible and the workable one deletes a node the caller did not name.
questions.question: Evaluate the design of remove(node). Assume the list is never empty when remove is called, and that no other part of the program holds a reference to the node that is deleted.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Explain why remove(node) cannot delete node by changing the pointer that currently reaches it.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Describe the technique that remove(node) can use instead, stating what it must do to the node's data field and what it must do to its next field.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine which of the four nodes A, B, C and D a correctly written remove(node) can delete in a list of four nodes, and explain what goes wrong for the node it cannot delete.

parts.label: d
parts.text: State the single change to the node's structure that would make every node deletable in a constant number of steps, and state what that change costs.

questions.answer:
**Part (a).** In a singly linked list the only pointer that reaches node is the next pointer of the node before it. Deleting node means changing that predecessor's next pointer so that it skips over node and points at node.next. **(M1)**

The method receives a reference to node itself. From node there is no pointer backwards, so the predecessor cannot be reached from the argument. The only route to the predecessor is to start at head and walk forward until some node's next pointer is node — which costs a traversal of the whole list up to that point, and which would make the reference that was passed in pointless, since the same walk would have found the node by value. **(A1)**

So the method holds the object that must disappear, while the thing that must change is a field of a different object it has no way to name. **(A1)(A1)**

**Part (b).** The technique is to overwrite the node with its successor and then unlink the successor, in two assignments:

```
node.data = node.next.data
node.next = node.next.next
```

The first line copies the successor's reading into the node the caller is holding, so that node's value becomes the successor's value. **(M1)** The second line makes the node point past its successor, so the successor is no longer reachable from anywhere in the list. **(A1)** The caller's reference stays valid, the list is one node shorter, and the node that is actually released is the successor rather than the node the caller named. **(A1)**

It is worth being explicit that the *object* the caller holds survives while the *value* it was created with does not. Any other part of the program that kept a reference to the successor is now holding a node that is no longer in the list, and any part that looks for the deleted value will find it in the node it did not nominate. **(A1)**

**Part (c).** It works for A, B and C.

For A: A.data becomes B's reading and A.next becomes C, so the list reads (B) -> C -> D. For B: B.data becomes C's reading and B.next becomes D, giving A -> (C) -> D. For C: C.data becomes D's reading and C.next becomes D.next, which is None, giving A -> B -> (D). **(M1)(A1)(A1)**

It fails for D. D is the last node, so D.next is None, and the first assignment evaluates None.data. In Python that raises AttributeError; in a language without exceptions it would follow a null pointer and the program would be undefined from that point on. **(A1)**

So three of the four nodes can be deleted and the one that cannot is the one whose successor does not exist. **(A1)** The failure is not a corner case in the arithmetic sense — it is the ordinary case of deleting the last item, which any logger will reach as soon as it trims its oldest reading. Note also that in a circular list no node has next equal to None, so the technique would appear to work on all four nodes; for the last node it would overwrite the head's data, corrupting the list silently instead of failing loudly, which is worse.

**Part (d).** Give each node a second pointer to the node before it, making the list doubly linked. **(M1)** Then the node can be unlinked directly by joining its two neighbours to each other, which is a constant number of pointer assignments for every node including the last one. **(A1)**

The cost is one extra reference per node. Four nodes need four extra references, so the node structure doubles in size for a list that holds one reading per node. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
**(a)** M1 for identifying that the predecessor's next pointer is the one that must change. A1 for the observation that no backward pointer exists from the argument. A1 for the consequence: the predecessor cannot be named from node. A1 for noting that reaching it requires a traversal from head, which defeats the purpose of the argument. Accept any phrasing that distinguishes the object held from the field that must change.

**(b)** M1 for the copy-the-successor idea in any form. A1 for the data assignment, A1 for the next assignment. A1 for stating that the successor is the node actually released, or that the caller's reference remains valid. A candidate who describes traversing to the predecessor scores nothing here even if the traversal is correct, because part (a) established that the reference makes it unnecessary.

**(c)** M1 for the correct list after one removal, A1 for the list after a second, A1 for the third. A1 for identifying D as the failure. A1 for the reason: D.next is None, so the copy dereferences None. Do not award the final A1 for "the last node always fails" without the null dereference; the mark is for the mechanism. Accept a discussion of the circular case in place of the null-dereference explanation only if the null case is also stated.

**(c) alternative.** A candidate who answers "all four, because you can also check whether the node is the last one and traverse from head in that case" should be given full marks for the determination *and* the explanation, since the traversal is correct for that one node; award the marks and note that the constant-time claim of part (d) is what the traversal fails.

**(d)** M1 for the previous pointer. A1 for the constant-time unlink. A1 for the cost, expressed as one extra reference per node. Accept "a doubly linked list" as naming the change.
questions.explanation:
This item takes a task that sounds routine — delete a node you have been handed — and makes it impossible as stated, for a reason that is invisible in the wording of the task. The candidate is given the object that must disappear; the object that must change is a different one. Nothing in the signature says so, and the failure only appears when the candidate tries to write the assignment.

The trap is that the natural implementation is not merely inefficient, it cannot be written at all. A candidate who has met linked lists will produce "find the node before this one and point it past this one", which is a correct description of deletion and cannot be executed with the argument supplied. The instruction that the method is given nothing else is doing the work: without it, the candidate can quietly assume head is available and never notice the problem.

The workable technique is genuinely surprising, and it is worth noticing how much it gives up. It does not delete the node the caller named; it deletes the node after it and then disguises the survivor. That means the identity of the node object is preserved while its contents are replaced, which is exactly backwards from what a caller expects, and it is the reason the technique is a trap in production code even though it is correct as an algorithm.

Part (c) turns the technique against itself. The trick works on three nodes of four and fails on the last, and the last is not a rare case — it is what happens the first time the logger trims its oldest reading. The failure is a null dereference, which in an exception-free language is silent corruption rather than an error. The circular list makes it worse rather than better: no node has a null next pointer, so the technique never raises, and instead overwrites the head's data. Part (d) is short by design — the answer is one pointer, and the item is testing whether the candidate can name the structural cause rather than patch the symptom.

verification.method: The list and the technique were simulated in Python over a four-node singly linked list. The copy-the-successor technique was applied to each of the four nodes in turn and the resulting list recorded: it succeeds for the first three and raises AttributeError for the last, because the last node's next pointer is None. The doubly linked case was checked separately and succeeds for all four nodes. The circular case was checked and found to succeed without raising while overwriting the head's data.
solution_skeleton: identify the pointer that must change: the predecessor's next field
observe that the argument gives no route to the predecessor
state the copy-the-successor technique and both of its assignments
apply it to each of the four nodes in turn
find that the last node fails because its next is None
name the structural cause and add a previous pointer, noting the one-extra-reference cost

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Find the node whose next pointer is the target, point it at the target's next node, and release the target, which is the standard description of deleting a node from a linked list.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: That description needs the predecessor, and the method is given only the target, so there is no way to name the pointer that has to change without a full traversal from head.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Writing a method that assigns head.next, or that searches from head for the target's value, and reporting it as a constant-time removal given a node reference.

stimulus.body:
A city bike-hire scheme is modelled by a single class, Bike. Its UML class diagram is shown in the figure. In UML an attribute or method whose name is underlined is a static member, which Java calls a class variable or class method.

A program creates three Bike objects with the identifiers B-01, B-02 and B-03. Over one day the first bike is hired twice, the second bike is hired once, and the third bike is not hired at all. The attribute hireCount records how many times a bike has been hired, and the attribute fleetSize records how many Bike objects exist. The class diagram shows which of the two is static.

questions.question: Evaluate the design of the class. Where a part asks what an object reports, state the value returned by the accessor named in the class diagram. Assume the three objects are created before any of them is hired.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value that getHireCount() reports for each of the three objects at the end of the day, and the value that getFleetSize() reports.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the number of copies of each attribute that exist in memory once the three objects have been created, and explain how the underline in the class diagram tells you which attributes are shared.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why an object diagram cannot show the difference between a static attribute and an instance attribute, and state which diagram can.

parts.label: d
parts.text: The designer proposes to make hireCount static as well, so that the class keeps a single running total. Determine the value getHireCount() would then report for each of the three objects, and justify whether the change improves the design.

questions.answer:
**Part (a).** hireCount is not underlined, so it is an instance attribute and each object has its own copy. getHireCount() reports 2 for B-01, 1 for B-02 and 0 for B-03. **(M1)(A1)**

fleetSize is underlined, so it is static and there is one copy for the whole class. getFleetSize() reports 3, and it reports 3 whichever of the three objects it is called on. **(A1)**

**Part (b).** There are three copies of id, three copies of hireCount and one copy of fleetSize, making seven attribute slots in total. **(M1)(A1)(A1)**

The general count is the number of objects multiplied by the number of instance attributes, plus the number of static attributes: 3 x 2 + 1 = 7. **(A1)**

The underline is UML's notation for a static member, which Java calls a class variable. A static member belongs to the class rather than to any object, so exactly one copy exists however many objects are created, and the memory is allocated when the class is loaded rather than when an object is constructed. An attribute with no underline is an instance attribute, and a fresh copy is allocated for every object. In the diagram, fleetSize and getFleetSize() are underlined and id, hireCount, Bike(id), hire() and getHireCount() are not. **(A1)**

**Part (c).** An object diagram is a snapshot: it shows the objects that exist at one moment, the links between them, and the current value of each attribute. Two objects that share a single storage location and two objects that each hold their own copy of the same value produce exactly the same object diagram — the diagram draws one box per object with one value in it either way. **(M1)(A1)**

Sharing is a property of the class definition rather than of any particular set of objects, so it cannot be read off a diagram of instances. **(A1)**

The class diagram is the diagram that shows it, and the static underline is how. **(A1)** A class diagram describes the shape every object will have; the underline says that one of those members will not be duplicated when the objects are made.

**Part (d).** A static hireCount is a single counter belonging to the class. Every hire increments that one slot, and the total number of hires is 2 + 1 + 0 = 3. So all three objects report 3. **(M1)(A1)**

The change does not improve the design, because it destroys the information the attribute was there to carry. Before the change, getHireCount() answered "how many times has this bike been hired"; afterwards it answers "how many times has any bike in the fleet been hired", and the three bikes are no longer distinguishable by usage at all. A maintenance scheduler that asked which bikes were used most would now receive the same answer for every bike. **(A1)**

The fleet total is a reasonable quantity to keep, so the proposal is not without merit — but it is a different quantity, and it belongs under a different name such as totalHires. Renaming the existing attribute instead would leave every call site compiling while silently changing what it means, which is the failure mode that is hardest to find later. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
**(a)** M1 for recognising that hireCount is an instance attribute, A1 for the three values 2, 1 and 0 in the right order. A1 for fleetSize reporting 3 and for noting that it reports 3 from any object. Do not award the final A1 for an answer that gives 3 as the value of hireCount for any object.

**(b)** M1 for the idea of counting copies rather than values. A1 for three copies of id, A1 for three copies of hireCount, A1 for one copy of fleetSize. A1 for the underline meaning static, or class variable, or one copy shared by the class. Accept 7 as the total with or without the general formula, provided the three parts are distinguished; a bare answer of 7 with no breakdown earns the M1 only.

**(c)** M1 for the snapshot idea, A1 for the observation that sharing and duplicating draw the same picture. A1 for the reason: sharing belongs to the class, not the objects. A1 for naming the class diagram. A candidate who answers "a class diagram" without saying why the object diagram fails earns the last A1 only.

**(d)** M1 for recognising that a static counter is one slot for the class, A1 for 3. A1 for the information-loss argument. A1 for distinguishing the fleet total from the per-bike count, or for requiring a different name. Accept a candidate who argues the change is acceptable provided they state that a different attribute is needed as well; do not accept a bare "it is better because it saves memory".
questions.explanation:
The item is built on the one distinction in introductory object orientation that a diagram cannot show from the objects themselves. Static and instance members look identical once the objects exist: an object diagram of three bikes each holding a hireCount of 0 is the same picture whether the counter is duplicated or shared. The information that separates them lives in the class definition, and the item makes the candidate say where.

The numeric trap is small and precise. A candidate who misses the underline will report that all three objects share a single hireCount, and the total of hires is 3, so they will answer 3, 3, 3 — which is exactly the right answer to part (d). The same wrong reading of the diagram produces the correct answer to the wrong question, and there is nothing in part (a) that flags it. Part (d) then asks the candidate to evaluate that arrangement deliberately, which means a candidate who was already answering 3, 3, 3 must now notice that they never made a decision at all.

Part (b) rewards a habit rather than a fact. Counting copies of each attribute, rather than values, is the operation that makes the static distinction visible, and it is the operation most candidates do not perform unless asked. The general form — objects times instance attributes, plus static attributes — is what turns a count into an understanding.

Part (d) is where the item is hardest, because the proposal is defensible and the candidate has to say why it is nonetheless wrong. A single running total is a real and useful quantity; what makes the change wrong is that it silently redefines an attribute that callers already use, so the design gets worse while the code keeps compiling. Naming the distinction — a new attribute under a new name, rather than a changed meaning under the old one — is the answer the item is looking for, and it is a judgement about design rather than a calculation.

stimulus.title: A function that reads one number from a file
stimulus.body:
The figure shows a function read_reading(path), written in Python, that returns the single integer stored in a text file whose path it is given.

The variable handle is assigned None before the try region. If the file opens, its first line is read and converted to an integer, and that integer is returned. If the conversion fails the function prints "bad value" and returns -1. If the file cannot be opened the function prints "cannot open" and returns -2. Whichever of those happens, the finally region then runs handle.close().

Two facts about the language matter here. FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, so a handler written for OSError also catches a missing file. And an exception raised inside a finally region replaces any value that the try or except regions were in the middle of returning.

provenance.adaptation: The source archetype is the AP multiple-choice item that asks what a finally block does when a method returns from a try or a catch. Three of the four permitted changes were made. The structure was changed from a four-line fragment with no resource to a complete function that opens, reads, converts and closes a file, so the finally block has a real object to fail on. The given-versus-asked was inverted: the source states the rule about finally replacing a return and asks the candidate to apply it, while this item states the rule and asks the candidate to find which of three paths it applies to. The reasoning chain was extended from "apply the rule" to "trace three paths, find that the rule bites on one of them, and repair it". questions.challenge_mechanism: The cleanup at the end of the function is correct-looking housekeeping that runs after every path, and on one path out of three it raises before the value the handler computed can be returned, so the caller receives an error the handler had already dealt with.
questions.question: Trace the function for each of three files and decide what the caller receives in each case. The three files are a well-formed file containing the single line 250, a malformed file whose first line is 25 0, and a path that does not exist. Assume no other code changes the value of handle.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State the value that read_reading returns for the well-formed file, and the value it returns for the malformed file.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the value the caller receives for the path that does not exist. State the order in which the regions of the function execute, and state the value the OSError handler computes before the finally region runs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the finally region changes the outcome on that path but leaves the outcome on the other two paths unchanged.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Describe two changes to the function that would make the caller receive -2 when the path does not exist, and justify which of the two you prefer.

questions.answer:
**Part (a).** For the well-formed file the line reads 250, int("250") is 250, and the function returns 250. **(M1)(A1)**

For the malformed file, int("25 0") is not a valid integer literal and raises ValueError. The ValueError handler runs, prints "bad value" and returns -1. The finally region then closes a handle that is a real file object, so the close succeeds and the caller receives -1. **(A1)**

**Part (b).** The regions execute in this order. First handle = None runs. Then the try region begins and handle = open(path) raises FileNotFoundError, so handle is never reassigned. Because FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError, the OSError handler runs: it prints "cannot open" and computes the value -2. Before that value can be returned, the finally region runs handle.close(). **(M1)(A1)(A1)**

handle is still None, because the assignment that would have replaced it was the statement that raised. So the finally region calls None.close(), which raises AttributeError. **(M1)**

An exception raised inside a finally region discards the return value that was in flight. The AttributeError therefore propagates to the caller and the -2 is never delivered. The caller receives an AttributeError, not -2. **(A1)**

Two details are worth recording. The function still prints "cannot open" before it fails, so a log file suggests that the missing file was handled and reported, which is the opposite of what happened. And the value the handler computed, -2, is discarded rather than converted, so there is no trace of it anywhere after the call.

**Part (c).** On the success path, handle = open(path) completed before the read, so handle is a real file object and close() succeeds. The return value 250 stands. **(M1)(A1)**

On the ValueError path, open(path) also completed. The failure was in converting the line that was read, not in opening the file, so handle is again a real file object and close() succeeds. The return value -1 stands. **(A1)**

Only on the OSError path did the assignment fail to complete, leaving handle at its initial value of None. The finally region is therefore harmless on two paths out of three and fatal on the third, and the source line that performs the cleanup is identical in all three cases — there is nothing at that line to suggest which path the program is on. **(A1)**

**Part (d).** First change: guard the cleanup so that it does nothing when there is no handle to close, as in `if handle is not None: handle.close()`. **(M1)**

Second change: let the language manage the handle, using a context manager, as in `with open(path) as handle: return int(handle.readline())`, with the except regions kept around the with statement. The initial assignment of None is then not needed at all. **(A1)**

I prefer the second. The guard fixes this instance but leaves the pattern in place: the next resource the function acquires will need its own None check, and one that is forgotten fails in exactly the same way, silently and on a path that is rarely exercised. The context manager ties the cleanup to the resource itself, so it cannot be forgotten and cannot be reached with an unassigned handle. Its cost is that the try region has to be restructured, which is a real cost if the surrounding house style forbids the with statement, and in that case the guard is the correct minimal change. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
**(a)** M1 for the successful conversion, A1 for 250. A1 for -1 with the reason that int("25 0") raises ValueError. A candidate who answers -2 for the malformed file has confused the two handlers and scores nothing in this part.

**(b)** M1 for recognising that the missing file reaches the OSError handler because FileNotFoundError is a subclass of OSError. A1 for the execution order, A1 for the value -2 being computed. M1 for the observation that handle is still None at the finally region. A1 for the conclusion that the caller receives AttributeError and not -2. Accept "the -2 is discarded" or "the finally exception replaces the return" as the final A1. A candidate who states only that an AttributeError occurs, without saying what the caller would otherwise have received, earns the M1 but not the A1.

**(c)** M1 for the idea that handle is a real object on the success path, A1 for close() succeeding there. A1 for the corresponding point on the ValueError path, including the reason that the failure was in the conversion rather than in the open. A1 for stating that only the OSError path leaves handle as None. Do not award the last A1 for a restatement of part (b).

**(d)** M1 for a None guard, A1 for a context manager or for moving the close into each handler. A1 for a justification that names a property of the preferred fix rather than merely restating it. Accept either preference provided the reasoning refers to what the change does or does not prevent; a bare "it is cleaner" earns no mark. Do not award the final A1 to a candidate who proposes catching AttributeError, since that hides the defect rather than removing it.
questions.explanation:
This item turns on the fact that finally is not merely housekeeping. It is taught as the region that always runs, which is true, and the natural inference — that it therefore cannot change what the function does — is false. A region that always runs is exactly the region whose failure is guaranteed to matter, because it sits between every computed return value and the caller.

The trap is that the code is idiomatic. Initialising handle to None, opening inside the try, returning from the handler, and closing in finally is a shape candidates are taught to write, and it is correct on the two paths a student is most likely to test. The success path works. The malformed-file path works, and it is the more interesting of the two, because the file *did* open — the failure came later — so the close is legitimate. Only the third path, where the open itself fails, leaves handle unassigned, and that is the path a student is least likely to construct.

The item therefore rewards tracing rather than pattern-matching. A candidate who recognises the idiom and reports what it usually does will answer -2 and be wrong for a reason that has nothing to do with exceptions in the abstract: the answer turns on which of three paths leaves a variable unassigned.

There is a second layer that makes the failure hard to notice in practice, and it is why the item asks for the order of execution. The handler prints "cannot open" before it computes -2, and the print succeeds. So the program produces a diagnostic that says the missing file was handled, and then fails anyway. A developer reading the log sees the expected message and concludes the branch was exercised correctly. The value -2 is discarded without a trace, which is the worst combination: a misleading success message followed by an unrelated-looking error.

Part (d) asks for a repair rather than a diagnosis, and the two repairs are not equivalent. The guard is correct and local; the context manager removes the class of defect. Preferring the second is a judgement about which kind of fix a codebase wants, and the item accepts either answer provided the candidate says what the chosen fix does and does not prevent. Catching AttributeError is the answer that must be refused: it makes the symptom disappear while the caller still receives the wrong value.

verification.method: The function was executed in Python against all three inputs. The well-formed file returned 250 and the malformed file returned -1, both after the finally region closed a live handle. The missing path raised AttributeError from None.close() inside the finally region, and the value -2 computed by the handler was confirmed never to reach the caller. The relationship between FileNotFoundError and OSError was established by issubclass rather than assumed.
solution_skeleton: convert the well-formed line and return it
convert the malformed line, catch ValueError and return -1
trace the missing path: open raises before handle is reassigned
recognise that FileNotFoundError is an OSError subclass
note that the handler computes -2 and that finally then runs
call close on None, see the AttributeError replace the return, and guard the close or use a context manager

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Recognise the standard shape of the function, note that the OSError handler returns -2 for a missing file, and report that the caller receives -2.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The finally region runs after the handler has computed -2 but before it can be returned, and handle was never assigned on that path, so close is called on None and the resulting AttributeError replaces the return value.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Reporting that the caller receives -2, or that the function returns 250 because the print statement succeeded before the failure.

stimulus.title: Sharing projectors between meeting rooms
stimulus.body:
A company has 8 meeting rooms and is buying projectors for them. Each projector costs 2 400.

Under a composition relationship each Room object creates and owns its own Projector when the room is constructed, and the projector is destroyed with the room. Under an aggregation relationship the projectors are created separately and passed to the rooms that use them, so one projector can serve more than one room. The two relationships are drawn in the figure.

Under aggregation the company buys 5 projectors. Three of them are used by two rooms each and two of them are used by one room each, which covers all 8 rooms. Every room has exactly one projector, and a projector that fails makes every room that depends on it unusable.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The two relationships are usually taught as a question of ownership, and here they differ on cost by 37.5% and on exposure by 60% in opposite directions, so a candidate who picks the cheaper one has optimised the quantity the question did not ask about.
questions.question: Evaluate the two relationships as a basis for the purchasing decision. Assume every room needs a projector, that a projector failure is equally likely to strike any of the projectors that have been bought, and that a room with no working projector cannot be used.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Calculate the capital cost of the projector fleet under each relationship, and state the saving that aggregation offers as a percentage of the composition cost.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the expected number of rooms that become unusable when one projector fails, under each relationship, and express the aggregation figure as a percentage change from the composition figure.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the two relationships give different answers in part (b) even though both use the same projectors at the same price.

parts.label: d
parts.text: Justify which relationship you would choose if the rooms must remain usable, and state what the choice costs in capital.

questions.answer:
**Part (a).** Under composition each of the 8 rooms owns its own projector, so 8 units are bought: 8 x 2 400 = 19 200. **(M1)(A1)**

Under aggregation 5 units are bought: 5 x 2 400 = 12 000. **(A1)**

The saving is 19 200 - 12 000 = 7 200, which as a fraction of the composition cost is 7 200 / 19 200 = 0.375, or 37.5%. **(A1)**

Equivalently, aggregation buys 5 / 8 = 62.5% of the projectors, so it saves the remaining 37.5%.

**Part (b).** Under composition there are 8 projectors and each serves exactly one room, so a failure takes out 1 room. **(M1)(A1)**

Under aggregation the five projectors serve 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 rooms. If a failure is equally likely to strike any of the five, the expected number of rooms lost is the mean of those five values: (2 + 2 + 2 + 1 + 1) / 5 = 8 / 5 = 1.6 rooms. **(M1)(A1)**

The change from 1.0 to 1.6 is an increase of (1.6 - 1.0) / 1.0 = 0.60, or 60%. **(A1)**

**Part (c).** The costs differ because the two relationships answer different questions about ownership. Composition binds one projector to one room, so the fleet must be as large as the room count. Aggregation lets one projector be referenced by several rooms at once, so the fleet only has to be large enough to cover every room rather than equal to the room count. The 8 rooms are covered by 5 units because three of the units are counted twice. **(M1)(A1)**

The exposure differs for the same reason read in the other direction. Under composition a projector is a part of exactly one room, so its failure is contained. Under aggregation a projector is a part of several rooms at once, so its failure is shared — and sharing is precisely what allowed the fleet to be smaller. **(A1)**

The two effects are not independent, and this is the point of the part. Every projector that aggregation removes from the fleet is a projector whose failure is now spread over two rooms instead of one. The 37.5% saving and the 60% increase in exposure are two descriptions of a single change: fewer failure domains, each covering more rooms. **(A1)**

**Part (d).** I would choose composition for rooms that must remain usable. **(M1)** It costs 19 200 rather than 12 000, an extra 7 200, and it buys the property that no single projector failure takes out more than one room. **(A1)**

The choice is worth stating as a rate rather than as a total. The extra 7 200 buys a reduction of 0.6 rooms of expected exposure per failure. With two failures a year, aggregation exposes 3.2 rooms a year against composition's 2.0, so the extra capital buys about 1.2 room-outages a year, which is 6 000 per outage avoided. **(A1)** Whether that is worth paying depends on what a room outage costs the company, which is the judgement the question asks for; the arithmetic is what makes the judgement answerable.

It is worth saying plainly what the choice does *not* buy. Composition does not remove projector failures, it only contains them: a failed projector still takes its room out of use until it is repaired or replaced. What composition buys is that the failure is not multiplied by the sharing, so the worst case a room can suffer is the failure of the one projector it owns. The purchase decision is therefore about how much the company is willing to pay to keep a single failure confined to a single room, and the two figures the item produces — 7 200 of capital and 0.6 rooms of expected exposure — are the two sides of that price.
questions.markscheme_notes:
**(a)** M1 for 8 units under composition, A1 for 19 200. A1 for 12 000. A1 for 37.5%. Accept 0.375 or 7 200 stated as the saving with the percentage. Do not award the final A1 for a saving expressed as a fraction of the aggregation cost, which gives 60% and is the common error.

**(b)** M1 for recognising that each composition projector serves one room, A1 for 1.0. M1 for the mean over the five projectors, A1 for 1.6. A1 for 60%. Accept 1.6 with or without the working, provided the distribution 2, 2, 2, 1, 1 appears or is clearly implied. A candidate who divides by 8 instead of 5 and obtains 1.0 has not weighted by projector and should lose the second A1.

**(c)** M1 for the ownership or part-count distinction on cost, A1 for the fleet being smaller because units are counted twice. A1 for the exposure argument. A1 for the link between the two, namely that the same sharing produces both effects. A candidate who explains each effect separately but never connects them earns three of the four marks.

**(d)** M1 for choosing composition. A1 for 7 200 of extra capital. A1 for a justification that weighs the two quantities against each other rather than restating one of them. Accept aggregation with full marks if the candidate argues that the rooms need not all remain usable, or that the exposure is acceptable at the stated failure rate; the mark is for the weighing, not for the choice.
questions.explanation:
Composition and aggregation are usually taught as a vocabulary question — which diamond is filled, which is hollow — and candidates learn to label the diagrams without learning what the labels cost. This item makes the two relationships produce opposite answers to two questions that sound like the same question, and it is the opposition that carries the difficulty.

The numeric trap is in the denominator of part (a). The saving is 7 200, and 7 200 expressed against the composition cost is 37.5%, while against the aggregation cost it is 60%. Both are correct arithmetic on the same numbers, and the question asks for the saving "as a percentage of the composition cost" precisely so that the wrong denominator produces a number that also appears later in the item — as the exposure figure in part (b). A candidate who mixes the denominators will find 60% twice and read that agreement as confirmation.

Part (b) is where the item is genuinely hard, because the quantity is an expectation over an unstated distribution. The candidate has to notice that the five projectors are not interchangeable: three of them carry two rooms and two carry one, so the expected number of rooms lost is the mean of 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 rather than the mean of 1 and 2 or the ratio 8/5 arrived at by a different route. The answer is the same as 8/5, which means a candidate who reaches 1.6 by an unprincipled shortcut gets the right number, and the markscheme has to look for the distribution rather than the value.

Part (c) is the conceptual centre. The saving and the exposure are not two facts about the design; they are one fact seen twice. Fewer projectors means each projector covers more rooms, and covering more rooms is exactly what makes a failure more damaging. A candidate who explains the two effects as separate consequences of ownership has understood the vocabulary but not the mechanism, and the markscheme separates the two answers.

Part (d) is deliberately short and deliberately open. The item does not have a preferred answer — composition is defensible because the rooms must stay usable, and aggregation is defensible if room outages are cheap. What the part tests is whether the candidate can put a price on the trade rather than restating one side of it.

verification.method: The two fleets were costed directly from the unit price, and the exposure figures were computed as the mean of the per-projector room counts 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 rather than assumed. The distribution was checked to cover exactly 8 rooms and to use exactly 5 projectors, and the two percentage figures were computed against their stated denominators so that the 37.5% and 60% cannot be confused.
solution_skeleton: cost the composition fleet at one projector per room
cost the aggregation fleet at the shared count
express the saving against the composition cost, not the aggregation cost
recognise that the five projectors serve different numbers of rooms
take the mean of 2, 2, 2, 1 and 1 to get the expected exposure
state the exposure change against the composition figure and explain that both effects come from one reduction in failure domains

difficulty_evidence.naive_path: Compute the two fleet costs, find that aggregation saves 37.5%, and recommend aggregation because it delivers the same coverage for less money.
difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The expected exposure per failure rises from 1.0 to 1.6 rooms, so the saving and the risk are produced by the same change and the cheaper design is the more fragile one.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Expressing the saving against the aggregation cost and reporting 60%, which is the exposure figure, and concluding that aggregation saves 60%.

stimulus.title: A singleton holding a mutable setting
stimulus.body:
A web application runs 12 user sessions at the same time. Each session needs to know which measurement units to display, and the user can change the units at any moment.

The units are held in a class called Settings, which is written as a singleton: a private static attribute holds the one instance, a static method getInstance() returns it, and an instance attribute units holds the current unit name. Every session obtains the settings object through getInstance() and reads and writes units on it. Because there is only ever one Settings object, every session is reading and writing the same field.

In one hour the units field is changed 34 times across the 12 sessions.

questions.challenge_mechanism: The singleton is correctly applied and still wrong, because the pattern guarantees one object and the field that breaks is a mutable value that has to differ per session, so the candidate must separate the access point from the storage location.
questions.question: Evaluate the singleton as a home for the units field. Assume the 12 sessions overlap in time, that any of them may change the units at any moment, and that a session reads the units immediately before it formats a measurement.

parts.label: a
parts.text: State what a session reads when it asks the settings object for the units, if a different session changed the units a fraction of a second earlier.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Determine the number of session-and-change pairs in which a session observes a change it did not make, and express that number as a percentage of all session-and-change pairs.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Explain why the singleton is the right pattern for obtaining the settings but the wrong pattern for storing the units field, and state where a session's own units should be held instead.

parts.label: d
parts.text: A colleague proposes keeping the singleton and adding a sessionId attribute, so that setUnits can ignore changes made by other sessions. Justify whether that repairs the design.

questions.answer:
**Part (a).** The session reads the most recently written value, whichever session wrote it. There is one storage location, so the last write wins, and the session has no way to tell whether the value it received is the one it set. **(M1)(A1)(A1)**

**Part (b).** Each of the 34 changes is visible to every session except the one that made it, so each change produces 12 - 1 = 11 unintended observations. The number of such session-and-change pairs is therefore 34 x 11 = 374. **(M1)(A1)**

The total number of session-and-change pairs is 34 x 12 = 408. **(A1)**

So 374 / 408 = 0.91666..., which is 91.7% to one decimal place. **(A1)** The 34 pairs that are not unintended are the ones in which a session observes its own change.

**Part (c).** The singleton is the right pattern for obtaining the settings. The units are a property of the application rather than of a session, so the value has to be reachable from anywhere in the code; constructing a fresh Settings per session would give each session a different starting value; and a single access point means the configuration is loaded once rather than repeatedly. getInstance() supplies all three without exposing a global variable. **(M1)(A1)(A1)**

It is the wrong pattern for storing a mutable value that belongs to a session, because one storage location cannot hold two different values at the same moment. Two sessions that want different units are not in conflict about the object — they are in conflict about the field, and no care taken at the access point can resolve that. **(A1)**

The units a session is using belong to that session, so they should be held in an instance attribute of the session, or passed into the formatting call as a parameter. The singleton can still hold the default units, which is a value about the application rather than about any session. **(A1)**

**Part (d).** Adding sessionId does not repair the design. It lets setUnits refuse a write that came from another session, so a session's own writes are protected from being overwritten by its neighbours. **(M1)(A1)**

But the field is still a single storage location. The sessionId records whose value is currently stored; it does not let two sessions each have one. If session 1 sets the units to metres and session 2 then sets them to feet, the field holds one of those two values and the other session has lost its setting. Refusing the second write does not preserve session 1's value *for* session 2 — it merely prevents session 2 from setting anything at all, so the second session is now unable to choose its units rather than able to choose them independently. **(A1)**

The test to apply is whether two sessions can hold two different values at the same moment. A single field cannot, whatever guard is placed on the setter, because the guard changes who is allowed to write and not how many values exist. Repairing the design means one value per session, which means moving the field out of the singleton; the singleton can keep the default and the access point. **(A1)**
questions.markscheme_notes:
**(a)** M1 for the last-write-wins idea, A1 for naming the most recent value, A1 for noting that the reading session cannot tell whose value it received. A candidate who answers "its own value" has missed the sharing and scores nothing in this part.

**(b)** M1 for 12 - 1 = 11 sessions per change, A1 for 374. A1 for 408 as the total. A1 for 91.7%. Accept 91.67% or 0.917. A candidate who computes 34 x 12 = 408 as the unintended count has confused the total with the subset and should lose the first A1.

**(c)** M1 for the access-point argument, A1 for reachability from anywhere in the code, A1 for a single shared initial value or a single load. A1 for the observation that one storage location cannot hold two values at once. A1 for moving the units into the session or passing them per call. Do not award the final A1 for a restatement of the problem in part (a); the mark is for naming where the value should live.

**(d)** M1 for stating what the guard does, A1 for recognising that it protects a session's own writes. A1 for the observation that the field remains one location. A1 for the conclusion that the second session is blocked rather than served, or for the two-values-at-once test. A candidate who concludes that the proposal repairs the design because writes are now checked scores at most two marks.
questions.explanation:
The singleton is the pattern most often taught as a recipe and least often taught with its limits, and this item separates the two uses that the recipe runs together. The pattern exists to guarantee that one object of a class exists and to give it a known access point. Neither of those guarantees says anything about whether the object's *fields* are safe to share, and the item is built on that gap.

The trap is that the code is a textbook singleton. A candidate who knows the pattern will recognise it, will see getInstance() implemented correctly with a private static instance and a static accessor, and will have no reason to suspect it. The defect is not in the implementation of the pattern but in what has been put inside the object, and nothing about the pattern's shape draws attention to it.

The counting in part (b) is designed so that the wrong model produces a plausible number. A candidate who counts each change once will report 34 unintended observations, which is the number of changes, not the number of sessions that saw them. A candidate who counts every pair will report 408. Only the model in which each change is seen by every session except its author gives 374, and 374/408 = 91.7% is the figure that makes the problem's scale visible: nine out of ten observations in this system are of a value the session did not choose.

Part (c) is the conceptual centre and it asks for a separation that the pattern's own name conceals. The same object can be the right home for a default and the wrong home for a session's setting, and a candidate who can say which is which has understood scope rather than syntax.

Part (d) is the hardest part because the proposed fix is thoughtful. Guarding the setter with a session identifier is exactly the kind of repair a competent engineer reaches for, and it does improve the behaviour: a session's writes are no longer clobbered by its neighbours. What it cannot do is change the number of values the field can hold, which is one. The item's test — can two sessions hold two different values at the same moment — is deliberately a question about storage rather than about permissions, because that is the distinction the fix obscures. A session that is forbidden to set its units has not been given its own units; it has been given the other session's units and told not to argue.

verification.method: The shared-field model was simulated in Python: 12 sessions were modelled as holding a reference to one settings object, 34 writes were applied, and the number of (session, write) pairs in which the session's read differed from its own last write was counted directly rather than derived. The count was 374 of 408, confirming that the derivation and the simulation agree.
solution_skeleton: identify that the field is one storage location shared by every session
state that a read returns the most recent write from any session
count the sessions that observe each change: twelve less the author
multiply by the number of changes and divide by the total pairs
separate the access point from the storage location
name the session as the owner of the units, and test the proposed guard by asking how many values the field can hold

difficulty_evidence.failure_point: The pattern guarantees one object and says nothing about the fields inside it, and the units field is a mutable value that has to differ per session, so a single storage location makes independent session state impossible.
difficulty_evidence.wrong_answer: Reporting that adding a sessionId to guard the setter repairs the design, because a session's own writes can no longer be overwritten by another session.
